kv.memory.bd-unclaim-resets-status-use-a: bd unclaim RESETS STATUS TO OPEN -- never use it to clear a stale claim on a 'blocked' bead, because 'blocked' is a STORED status in beads, not derived from dependencies. Unclaiming a blocked bead clears the assignee AND flips it to open, so it lands in 'bd ready' as falsely workable while its dependencies are still unmet. Use 'bd update <id> --assignee ""' instead: it clears the assignee, leaves status untouched, and is NOT subject to the actor-mismatch refusal that blocks both unclaim and close on a bead held by another actor (no --force needed). Context: bd HAS lease machinery -- 'bd heartbeat' refreshes, 'bd reclaim' reaps dead workers -- but reclaim only sees IN_PROGRESS issues with expired leases, so a claim that outlives a status change back to open/blocked is invisible to recovery; that was how five PKIX beads sat unworkable for six months with 'bd doctor' reporting 14/14 checks passed. Leave assignees on CLOSED beads alone: there they record who did the work rather than blocking anyone.
kv.memory.determinable-vs-consumer-shape: When grinding a hardening epic, sort the issues into 'determinable' and 'consumer-shaped' and treat them differently. Determinable = an RFC, a monotonicity property, or plain logic fixes the right answer (OCSP thisUpdate monotonicity, lock-poisoning recovery, clock-per-check instead of a captured timestamp, cache field privacy). Build those. Consumer-shaped = the right answer depends on what a consumer needs to emit or call, and no consumer exists yet (a telemetry observer: which fields -- latency, HTTP status, bytes, cache hit rate? a batch API: concurrency, ordering, partial-failure semantics?). Do NOT invent those blind; you commit public API in a guessed shape and then keep it for compatibility. Instead record the analysis on the bead -- what the channel options are, why the obvious one is blocked, what is already possible with existing public API -- so the design is cheap when a consumer turns up. PKIX-cr8: built 8, deferred 2 on exactly this line.
kv.memory.don-t-duplicate-isn-t-the-rule: Don't duplicate' isn't the rule -- 'don't duplicate code where a divergence would be a security bug' is. Two calls one day apart in the MTA-STS work went opposite ways and both were right: EXTRACTED pkix-aia-http's destination policy into pkix-net-guard (subtle address classification -- NAT64, IPv4-mapped, RFC 6598 -- where a second copy silently wrong is an SSRF hole), but did NOT extract pkix-dane-resolver's UpstreamConfig (parsing a name server address; a second copy can't cause a security bug, and sharing it would mean depending on pkix-dane + pkix-dnssec-anchor to parse a SocketAddr). Test for the distinction: would a divergence between the copies be exploitable, or merely untidy?
kv.memory.duplicated-beads-the-refiling-: Before superseding a duplicated bead, compare the two descriptions by LENGTH -- the re-filing is usually the empty one. In PKIX, 10 of 10 duplicated pairs had a re-filing of 16-115 chars (often literally 'Old: PKIX-xxx') against an original of 783-3733 chars holding the real analysis: file/line refs, expected vs actual, options with a recommendation. Running 'bd supersede <original> --with=<refiling>' would have destroyed ~19,000 characters of reading. Correct merge runs the OTHER way: keep the re-filing (it is parented to the live epic, not a finished review pass), copy the original's description into it verbatim with a provenance line, then close the original. Also reconcile priority by taking the HIGHER of the two -- the same pattern hid a P0 at P2 (PKIX-q9hv.2 vs PKIX-4ca.3), where the re-filing dropped the analysis AND dropped two priority levels. One-liner to spot it: compare len(description) in .beads/issues/*.json for each pair.
kv.memory.forwarding-impls-technique-and:
Forwarding impls (impl Trait for &T / Arc<T> / Box<T>) -- the technique and the hazard, two sides of one thing.

TECHNIQUE: they are the non-breaking escape from a by-value + Clone trait bound. pkix-path's SignatureVerifier was takeable only by value and every consumer also needed Clone, so a verifier owning a hardware token or open session was unusable. The listed options were all breaking (add a lifetime to CrlChecker, switch to &V, make Arc canonical). Adding 'impl SignatureVerifier for &T' fixed it with no signature change: &T is Copy, so Clone is satisfied and nothing is duplicated. Arc<T> covers the no-borrow-to-hold case. Gate an Arc impl on std in a no_std crate -- alloc::sync needs atomic CAS, so an unconditional impl silently locks out thumbv6m-type targets.

HAZARD: adding a DEFAULTED method to a trait that already has a forwarding impl silently breaks it. The forwarding impl keeps compiling and the new method falls through to the default, so Arc<Inner> quietly loses whatever Inner's override provided -- and the default is usually a correct-but-weaker implementation, which is what makes it invisible. Hit when put_crl_unless_rollback moved onto RevocationCache: Arc<dyn RevocationCache> (the documented sharing shape) would have dropped from a single-lock compare-and-insert to a racy get-then-put.

RULE both ways: grep every 'impl .* Trait for' when touching a trait, and test THROUGH each wrapper shape by counting calls into an overriding impl -- no other test can see the difference.
kv.memory.mta-sts-and-dane-need-opposite: MTA-STS and DANE need OPPOSITE resolver configurations in the same workspace, and both are correct. pkix-dane-resolver sets hickory validate=true and refuses unvalidated answers (RFC 7672 §2.1.1: indeterminate TLSA == insecure; DANE's trust basis IS DNSSEC). pkix-mta-sts-resolver must NOT require DNSSEC (RFC 8461 §1 relies on CAs and 'does not require DNSSEC, at a cost of risking malicious downgrades'; the _mta-sts TXT record carries no authentication at all -- it's a change token pointing at a policy whose trust comes from the HTTPS cert). Requiring validation there would refuse policies from most conforming domains. Same for profiles: MTA-STS §4.2 requires a SAN so BasicTlsProfile is right, while SMTP DANE per RFC 7672 §3.2.3 consults commonName so BasicSmtpMtaProfile requires neither SAN nor EKU.
kv.memory.mutation-testing-assert-the-ma:
When proving a new test actually catches the bug it guards, by reverting the fix and expecting a failure, ASSERT THE PATTERN MATCH COUNT FIRST. A mutation that silently fails to apply leaves the test passing against correct code, which looks like confirmation and proves nothing. This bit three times in one session on PKIX:

- "Some(Err(e)) => return Err(e)," appears 3x in pkix-path-builder/src/lib.rs (1013 build_path_with_config, 1163 and 1196 build_first_valid_path_with_config). Only 1163 is on the path a build_first_valid_path test drives.
- "verifier\n        .verify_signature(" appears 2x in pkix-chain/src/lib.rs (1499 verify_responder_is_delegated_by, 1862 signed_by).
- Reverting a threaded-through parameter to a hardcoded value leaves the parameter unused, so under RUSTFLAGS="-D warnings" the build FAILS instead of running the test -- and a grep for test results then returns nothing, which reads like a pass. Add "let _ = param;" to keep it compiling.

Practice that works: python with "assert s.count(old) == 1" before replacing, and when the count is not 1, resolve which site is live with
  for L in $(grep -n PATTERN file | cut -d: -f1); do awk -v n=$L "NR<=n && /^pub fn |^fn /{f=\$0} END{print f}" file; done
then mutate by LINE INDEX, not by string. Always cp the file to the scratchpad first and restore with cp, then confirm restoration with git diff --stat showing no change.

Why it matters here: every nontrivial fix in this workspace gets its test mutation-verified before the bead is closed, and the close reason cites that verification. A silent non-apply would put a false claim in the bead.
kv.memory.rustflags-d-warnings-not-inher: CI parity needs BOTH: RUSTFLAGS=-D warnings AND RUSTDOCFLAGS=-D warnings. RUSTFLAGS does NOT reach rustdoc, so a broken or private intra-doc link is only a warning locally while quality-gates (which sets both workflow-wide) fails on it. That exact gap broke the gate on 2bdf3216: public docs on CachedHttpOcspFetcher linked to the private fn is_staler_ocsp, and a local 'RUSTFLAGS=-D warnings cargo doc --all-features' passed. Clippy also does NOT run in the bare-metal or feature-combination jobs, so an unused import or a dead pub(crate) item is a warning locally and an error there -- and it bites hardest on cfg-gated code, where an item used only by feature-gated code is dead in the no-feature build (pkix-tlsrpt classify imports, pkix-aia-http is_public, time::Clock in pkix-revocation-http). Full local gate: export RUSTFLAGS='-D warnings' RUSTDOCFLAGS='-D warnings'; cargo fmt --all --check; cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features; cargo doc --workspace --all-features --no-deps; cargo hack check --workspace --feature-powerset --depth 2 -- WORKSPACE-wide, never per-crate.
kv.memory.verify-the-bead-premise-not-ju: Verify a review bead's stated premise before implementing its proposed fix -- the reasoning in old review notes is wrong often enough to matter, and these beads are mine from earlier passes, not gospel. Three in one session: PKIX-f1j4.18 argued client-ureq should imply crl+ocsp because 'features are additive, an explicit crl=true wins' -- that is not how Cargo resolves, the implication cannot be subtracted and would force x509-ocsp/sha1/sha2 on CRL-only consumers, so the proposed fix was the wrong one. PKIX-f1j4.19 was marked 'opinion, skip if disagreeing' but was a latent trap: the comparator's parameter names were inverted at its only call site, correct behaviour behind a lying signature. PKIX-f1j4.13 listed three options, all breaking or no-ops, and missed the additive one. Earlier: a bead I filed guessing ureq would surface Error::Rustls was wrong (it uses Error::Io with a concrete rustls::Error in get_ref). Read the code and re-derive the argument; a bead's priority label and its reasoning are both just a previous reading.
kv.memory.when-a-documented-gap-gets-clo: When a documented gap gets closed, INVERT the test that pinned it rather than deleting it. pkix-tlsrpt had a test asserting NOTHING maps to sts-webpki-invalid (because FetchError::Transport conflated a TLS failure with a network one). After adding FetchError::TlsValidation, the test became 'only TlsValidation maps to it, and Transport explicitly does not' -- the harm guarded against never changed, only the ability to distinguish the cases. A future change folding the variants back together still fails there.
